column1: Under APA § 551(1), what makes something an "agency"?
column2:
It is an authority of the federal government, meaning it can take final and binding action.

Outline 0.1

column1: Why isn't the President treated as an "agency" under the APA?
column2:
APA review of the President would raise Article II problems (constitutional avoidance).

Outline 0.1

column1: What decides whether an office is an APA "agency," given that size doesn't?
column2:
Its responsibilities. A one-person office can be an agency.

Outline 0.1

column1: What is an agency's "organic statute"?
column2:
The act that creates, empowers, defines, and limits the agency.

Outline 0.2

column1: Who can abolish an agency Congress created?
column2:
Only Congress. Born by Congress, must die by Congress; the President can only hollow it out.

Outline 0.2

column1: What test does the Court use today for nondelegation?
column2:
The intelligible principle test.

Outline Part I

column1: Rehnquist's NDD test (Benzene), element 1 of 3: Congress must ___.
column2:
Make the important choice of social policy itself.

Outline Part I, Consideration 1

column1: Rehnquist's NDD test (Benzene), element 2 of 3: Congress must ___.
column2:
Supply an intelligible principle to guide the agency's discretion.

Outline Part I, Consideration 1

column1: Rehnquist's NDD test (Benzene), element 3 of 3: the principle must ___.
column2:
Be judicially reviewable, a standard a court can test the agency against.

Outline Part I, Consideration 1

column1: How high is the bar for an intelligible principle?
column2:
Very low. It fails only when Congress has entirely abdicated.

Outline Part I, Consideration 1

column1: Name two statutory standards that have passed as intelligible principles.
column2:
Any two of "just and reasonable" rates, "fair and equitable" prices, "excessive profit," and "unfair or inequitable distribution of voting power."

Outline Part I, Consideration 1

column1: Why does Larsen say the NDD "never died"?
column2:
Later doctrines are built around the same delegation worry: avoidance in Benzene, the removal cases, and the MQD.

Outline Part I, Consideration 1

column1: Which case is called the "death certificate" of the NDD?
column2:
Whitman v. American Trucking

Outline Part I; Case Bank A

column1: Which case is the closest the Court has come to reviving the NDD?
column2:
Gundy v. United States (2019)

Outline Part I; Case Bank A

column1: Which case held OSHA must first find a significant risk before setting the strictest feasible standard?
column2:
Industrial Union Dep't v. American Petroleum Inst. (the Benzene Case)

Case Bank A

column1: In Benzene, how did the Court avoid striking down § 6(b)(5)?
column2:
It read § 6(b)(5) together with § 3(8), which is constitutional avoidance.

Case Bank A

column1: What did Mistretta hold about the Sentencing Commission?
column2:
Congress may delegate the power to write binding sentencing guidelines to it, because the statute gave enough guidance.

Case Bank A

column1: What test did Scalia propose in his Mistretta dissent?
column2:
Is it a naked policy choice, or merely ancillary to an executive or judicial power?

Case Bank A

column1: In Gundy, what did the Court do before asking whether there was an intelligible principle?
column2:
It construed the statute: SORNA required the AG to apply it to all pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible.

Case Bank A

column1: Which case struck down the NIRA's "codes of fair competition" written by industry groups?
column2:
A.L.A. Schechter Poultry

Case Bank A

column1: What is the takeaway line from Schechter Poultry?
column2:
The only rule cannot be "make rules."

Case Bank A

column1: Which case first struck down a delegation of legislative power to a private actor?
column2:
Carter Coal

Case Bank A

column1: What effect does an intelligible principle have on a delegation of legislative power to a private entity?
column2:
None. It is unconstitutional anyway.

Outline Part I, Consideration 2

column1: Private-delegation test, question 1 of 2:
column2:
Is the entity really private?

Outline Part I, Consideration 2

column1: Private-delegation test, question 2 of 2:
column2:
Is it wielding legislative power, or something short of it?

Outline Part I, Consideration 2

column1: What may a private entity do in regulation without a delegation problem?
column2:
Advise, guide, take part in an industry vote, or even veto.

Outline Part I, Consideration 2

column1: What may a private entity never do in regulation?
column2:
Make or co-author rules.

Outline Part I, Consideration 2

column1: Which D.C. Circuit case held Amtrak could not co-write binding standards with the FRA?
column2:
Ass'n of American Railroads v. DOT

Case Bank A

column1: What two concerns about private delegation did Ass'n of American Railroads name?
column2:
It saps democratic accountability, and private entities pursue private gain rather than the public good.

Case Bank A

column1: What did Lebron hold about Congress labeling an entity "private"?
column2:
The label is relevant but not controlling. The Court decides.

Case Bank A

column1: Which case struck down the one-House legislative veto?
column2:
INS v. Chadha (1983)

Case Bank A

column1: Under Chadha, what makes an action "legislation"?
column2:
It has the purpose and effect of altering legal rights, duties, and relations of persons outside the legislative branch.

Case Bank A

column1: What does legislation require under Chadha?
column2:
Bicameralism and presentment.

Case Bank A

column1: Who wrote the functionalist dissent in Chadha?
column2:
Justice White.

Case Bank A

column1: Name three ways Congress may lawfully control a delegation.
column2:
Any three of: amend or override by statute, appropriations, legislative history, the CRA.

Outline Part I, Consideration 3

column1: Complete the principle: private companies can ___ but not co-author; Congress can ___ but not veto.
column2:
Veto; override.

Outline Part I, 3(f)

column1: Why does the CRA survive Chadha?
column2:
A CRA resolution passes both Houses and is signed by the President.

Outline Part I, 3(e)

column1: How long does Congress have to disapprove a rule under the CRA?
column2:
60 legislative days.

Outline Part I, 3(e)

column1: After a CRA disapproval, what can't the agency do?
column2:
Issue a "substantially similar" rule without new statutory authorization.

Outline Part I, 3(e)

column1: What kind of agency action can the CRA erase?
column2:
Rules only, not adjudications.

Outline Part I, 3(e)

column1: Who decides whether a rule is a "major rule" under the CRA?
column2:
OIRA, in the White House.

Outline Part I, 3(e)

column1: What annual economic effect makes a rule "major" under the CRA?
column2:
$100 million or more.

Appendix B, CRA § 804(2)

column1: Appointments analysis, question 1 of 3:
column2:
Is the person an officer at all?

Outline Part II

column1: Appointments analysis, question 2 of 3:
column2:
Is the officer inferior or principal?

Outline Part II

column1: Appointments analysis, question 3 of 3:
column2:
Is the inferior officer appointed by the President alone, a Court of Law, or a Head of Department?

Outline Part II

column1: How must a principal officer be appointed?
column2:
By the President with Senate advice and consent.

Outline Part II

column1: What appointment requirements apply to a mere employee (not an officer)?
column2:
None from the Appointments Clause.

Outline Part II

column1: Officer test, element 1 of 2 (Buckley):
column2:
Significant authority pursuant to the laws of the United States.

Outline Part II, Consideration 1

column1: Officer test, element 2 of 2 (Germaine, Lucia):
column2:
A continuing position established by law.

Outline Part II, Consideration 1

column1: What does "continuing" mean in the officer test?
column2:
Not transient or incidental. It need not be permanent.

Outline Part II, Consideration 1

column1: Which case held FEC members picked by the Speaker and President pro tem were unconstitutionally appointed?
column2:
Buckley v. Valeo (1976)

Case Bank B

column1: In Buckley, what power made the FEC commissioners officers?
column2:
Enforcement power, including the power to seek judicial relief.

Case Bank B

column1: Why can't the Necessary and Proper Clause save the FEC appointments in Buckley?
column2:
The Appointments Clause is a specific recipe, and a specific recipe must be followed.

Outline Part II, Consideration 1

column1: Morrison inferior-officer factor 1 of 4:
column2:
Is she removable by a higher executive officer?

Outline Part II, Consideration 2

column1: Morrison inferior-officer factor 2 of 4:
column2:
Does she perform only certain, limited duties?

Outline Part II, Consideration 2

column1: Morrison inferior-officer factor 3 of 4:
column2:
Is she limited in jurisdiction?

Outline Part II, Consideration 2

column1: Morrison inferior-officer factor 4 of 4:
column2:
Is she limited in tenure?

Outline Part II, Consideration 2

column1: What is Edmond's test for an inferior officer?
column2:
Whether she has a superior other than the President.

Outline Part II, Consideration 2

column1: Which case held the independent counsel was an inferior officer a court could appoint?
column2:
Morrison v. Olson (1988)

Case Bank B

column1: What was Scalia's main objection in Morrison on the inferior-officer point?
column2:
She was harder to remove than a principal officer, so she can't be "inferior."

Case Bank B

column1: Which case held SEC ALJs are officers?
column2:
Lucia v. SEC (2018)

Case Bank B

column1: In Lucia, who had chosen the ALJs, and why was that a problem?
column2:
SEC staff. Officers must be appointed by a Head of Department, here the Commission.

Case Bank B

column1: Why did the Lucia majority say SEC ALJs mattered even more than Freytag's special trial judges?
column2:
An SEC ALJ's decision can become final without Commission review.

Case Bank B

column1: In Lucia, why did Breyer want to decide on statutory grounds?
column2:
Calling ALJs officers threatens their removal protections under Free Enterprise Fund.

Case Bank B

column1: Which case held administrative patent judges couldn't issue final, unreviewable decisions?
column2:
United States v. Arthrex (2021)

Case Bank B

column1: What was the remedy in Arthrex?
column2:
Let the PTO Director review PTAB decisions.

Case Bank B

column1: What lesson does Arthrex teach about inferior status?
column2:
At-will removal isn't enough. The officer needs substantive supervision of her decisions.

Case Bank B

column1: Which case is the source of "diffusion of power carries with it a diffusion of accountability"?
column2:
United States v. Arthrex

Case Bank B

column1: Which case held the Tax Court's Chief Judge could appoint special trial judges?
column2:
Freytag v. Commissioner (1991)

Case Bank B

column1: In Freytag, the majority called the Tax Court a ___; Scalia called its Chief Judge a ___.
column2:
"Court of Law"; "Head of Department."

Case Bank B

column1: Per the Freytag majority, what kind of body counts as a "Court of Law" for appointments?
column2:
One that adjudicates under the law, not only Article III courts.

Outline Part II, Consideration 3

column1: What is a "Department" for Appointments Clause purposes?
column2:
A freestanding component of the Executive Branch, not inside any other component (Free Enterprise Fund).

Case Bank B

column1: Who is the "Head of Department" at the SEC?
column2:
The Commission, acting as a multi-member body.

Case Bank B

column1: When can Congress add new duties to an existing officer without a new appointment?
column2:
When they are germane to the old office and Congress isn't aggrandizing itself.

Outline Part II, Consideration 5

column1: Which case let commissioned military officers serve as military judges without reappointment?
column2:
Weiss v. United States

Case Bank B

column1: Under Noel Canning, how short a recess is too short for a recess appointment?
column2:
Fewer than 10 days.

Case Bank B

column1: Under Noel Canning, what kind of Senate session prevents a recess?
column2:
Pro forma sessions.

Case Bank B

column1: Under Noel Canning, must the vacancy arise during the recess, or can it arise earlier?
column2:
It can arise before the recess.

Case Bank B

column1: Textual removal options: 1 impeachment only · 2 ___ · 3 follows appointment · 4 Congress sets terms
column2:
Unlimited presidential removal (Vesting Clause).

Outline 3.0

column1: Textual removal options: 1 impeachment only · 2 President unlimited · 3 ___ · 4 Congress sets terms
column2:
Removal follows the mode of appointment (Senate concurrence).

Outline 3.0

column1: Textual removal options: 1 impeachment only · 2 President unlimited · 3 follows appointment · 4 ___
column2:
Congress sets the terms (Necessary and Proper Clause).

Outline 3.0

column1: Which removal option did Myers adopt, and which does Slaughter return to?
column2:
Option 2, unlimited presidential removal, in both.

Outline 3.0

column1: Which removal option did Humphrey's Executor open the door to?
column2:
Option 4, Congress sets the terms.

Outline 3.0

column1: Which case upheld President Wilson removing a postmaster without the Senate?
column2:
Myers v. United States (1926)

Case Bank C

column1: Which two clauses did Myers combine to find unlimited removal power?
column2:
The Vesting Clause and the Take Care Clause.

Case Bank C

column1: Which case barred FDR from removing an FTC commissioner at will?
column2:
Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935)

Case Bank C

column1: Why didn't Myers control in Humphrey's Executor?
column2:
The FTC was quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial, not purely executive.

Case Bank C

column1: What for-cause language appeared in Humphrey's (and again in Seila Law)?
column2:
"Inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office."

Case Bank C

column1: Which case overruled Humphrey's Executor, and when?
column2:
Trump v. Slaughter, June 29, 2026 (6–3).

Case Bank C

column1: What does Humphrey's still cover after Slaughter?
column2:
Only entities exercising no part of the executive power.

Case Bank C

column1: Under Slaughter, what three agency functions all count as executive power?
column2:
Rulemaking, enforcement, and in-house adjudication that is part of an enforcement scheme.

Case Bank C

column1: What founding-era concept did Slaughter use to read history as settling removal?
column2:
Liquidation: a regular course of practice settled the President's removal power.

Case Bank C

column1: Slaughter reservations, 1 of 4:
column2:
Entities exercising no executive power.

Case Bank C

column1: Slaughter reservations, 2 of 4:
column2:
The Federal Reserve.

Case Bank C

column1: Slaughter reservations, 3 of 4:
column2:
Non–Article III courts such as the Tax Court.

Case Bank C

column1: Slaughter reservations, 4 of 4:
column2:
Inferior officers.

Case Bank C

column1: Which same-day 2026 case kept for-cause protection for Federal Reserve Governors?
column2:
Trump v. Cook (5–4)

Case Bank C

column1: Under Trump v. Cook, what must "cause" for removing a Fed Governor imply?
column2:
Unfitness for office, not a wish for a "more congenial replacement."

Case Bank C

column1: Which case is the paradigm of Congress giving itself a role in removal?
column2:
Bowsher v. Synar

Case Bank C

column1: Which case struck down two layers of for-cause removal?
column2:
Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (2010)

Case Bank C

column1: Why are two layers of for-cause removal unconstitutional (Free Enterprise Fund)?
column2:
The President can't hold the SEC accountable for the Board, so nobody he controls controls it.

Case Bank C

column1: Which case struck down for-cause protection for a single-director agency?
column2:
Seila Law LLC v. CFPB (2020)

Case Bank C

column1: Besides the single director, what feature of the CFPB troubled the Seila Law majority?
column2:
Budget independence: funded through the Fed, not appropriations.

Case Bank C

column1: What was the remedy in Seila Law?
column2:
Sever the removal restriction. The Director became removable at will.

Case Bank C

column1: Free Enterprise Fund vs. Seila Law: what structural feature does each condemn?
column2:
FEF: double for-cause layers. Seila: a single director with for-cause protection.

Outline 3.2, Step 4

column1: Which case, with Morrison, supports removal limits for inferior officers?
column2:
United States v. Perkins

Case Bank C

column1: Post-Slaughter, what is the key question in a removal problem?
column2:
Does the officer exercise executive power?

Outline 3.2, Step 3

column1: What remedy does the Court usually use when a removal restriction is unconstitutional?
column2:
Severance of the restriction.

Outline 3.2, Step 5

column1: What is the core claim of the unitary executive theory?
column2:
All executive power is vested in one person, so the President must control all executive discretion.

Outline 3.3

column1: Which case gave the President exclusive power to recognize foreign governments?
column2:
Zivotofsky v. Kerry

Case Bank C

column1: Exceptions to Article III adjudication, 1 of 4:
column2:
Territorial courts.

Outline 4.0

column1: Exceptions to Article III adjudication, 2 of 4:
column2:
Courts-martial (Dynes v. Hoover).

Outline 4.0

column1: Exceptions to Article III adjudication, 3 of 4:
column2:
Claims against the United States.

Outline 4.0

column1: Exceptions to Article III adjudication, 4 of 4:
column2:
Public rights that pass Schor/Stern balancing.

Outline 4.0

column1: Which case first recognized the public-rights exception?
column2:
Murray's Lessee

Case Bank D

column1: Which case approved agency adjudication generally, in dicta?
column2:
Crowell v. Benson

Case Bank D

column1: Schor factor 1 of 5:
column2:
How broad is the agency's adjudicative jurisdiction?

Outline 4.2

column1: Schor factor 2 of 5:
column2:
How much Article III supervision (standard of review, finality)?

Outline 4.2

column1: Schor factor 3 of 5:
column2:
Is it a public or private right?

Outline 4.2

column1: Schor factor 4 of 5:
column2:
What concerns drove Congress to depart from Article III?

Outline 4.2

column1: Schor factor 5 of 5:
column2:
Did the parties consent to this forum?

Outline 4.2

column1: Which case let the CFTC decide a state-law counterclaim the parties chose to bring there?
column2:
CFTC v. Schor (1986)

Case Bank D

column1: What fact about Schor himself cut against his Article III claim?
column2:
He chose the CFTC forum, then complained when he lost.

Case Bank D

column1: Which case held a bankruptcy court couldn't enter final judgment on a state-law tortious-interference counterclaim?
column2:
Stern v. Marshall (2011)

Case Bank D

column1: How did Stern define a public right?
column2:
A right integrally related to a particular federal government action.

Case Bank D

column1: Under Northern Pipeline and Stern, what kind of claim is never a public right?
column2:
State-law claims.

Case Bank D

column1: Which case held a securities-fraud defendant facing civil penalties gets a jury?
column2:
SEC v. Jarkesy (2024)

Case Bank D

column1: Jarkesy jury test, step 1 of 2:
column2:
Is the claim legal in nature (remedy and common-law analogue)?

Outline 4.3

column1: Jarkesy jury test, step 2 of 2:
column2:
Does the public-rights exception apply?

Outline 4.3

column1: Under Jarkesy, when is a money remedy "legal" rather than equitable?
column2:
When it punishes or deters. Money that restores the status quo is equitable.

Outline 4.3

column1: Under Jarkesy, which half of the "legal in nature" inquiry matters more?
column2:
The remedy.

Outline 4.3

column1: Which case held OSHA penalties can be decided without a jury?
column2:
Atlas Roofing Co. v. OSHRC (1977)

Case Bank D

column1: How did Jarkesy distinguish Atlas Roofing?
column2:
Atlas was a regulatory-compliance claim, not one with a common-law analogue.

Case Bank D

column1: Which case is the controlling analogy in Jarkesy (fraudulent conveyance needs a jury)?
column2:
Granfinanciera v. Nordberg

Case Bank D

column1: Which case says the Seventh Amendment reaches a statutory claim that is "legal in nature"?
column2:
Tull v. United States

Case Bank D

column1: Schor vs. Jarkesy: what question does each answer?
column2:
Schor: may a non–Article III body decide this at all? Jarkesy: does the Seventh Amendment require a jury?

Outline 4.4

column1: Name three public rights that survive Jarkesy.
column2:
Any three of: customs, immigration, tariffs, public benefits and patents, OSHA compliance, Indian tribes, public lands.

Outline 4.3

column1: Who decides which APA quadrant an agency action falls in?
column2:
Congress, in the organic statute.

Outline 5.3

column1: Which APA section governs informal rulemaking?
column2:
§ 553

Outline 5.3

column1: Which APA sections govern formal hearings?
column2:
§§ 556–557

Outline 5.3

column1: Which APA provision governs informal adjudication?
column2:
§ 555(e)

Outline 5.3

column1: Which APA section governs formal adjudication?
column2:
§ 554 (with §§ 556–557).

Outline 5.3

column1: Under § 551(4), what time orientation must a rule have?
column2:
Future effect.

Outline 5.4

column1: Under § 551(4), what applicability may a rule have?
column2:
General or particular.

Outline 5.4

column1: What category of action is always a rule under § 551(4)?
column2:
Rate-setting (rates, wages, prices, corporate structures).

Outline 5.4

column1: What category of action is always an order under § 551(6), even though it's prospective?
column2:
Licensing.

Outline 5.4

column1: How does § 551(6) define an "order"?
column2:
A final disposition in a matter other than rulemaking: anything that isn't a rule.

Outline 5.4

column1: Which case required notice and a hearing before a paving assessment on one street's owners?
column2:
Londoner v. City and County of Denver (1908)

Case Bank E

column1: Which case held no hearing was needed for a 40% valuation increase on all Denver property?
column2:
Bi-Metallic Investment Co. v. State Board of Equalization (1915)

Case Bank E

column1: Londoner vs. Bi-Metallic: which features trigger a due-process hearing?
column2:
Action that is specific and backward-looking, substantially affecting a small group (Londoner).

Outline 5.5

column1: Why is no hearing required in a Bi-Metallic situation?
column2:
People are "heard" through the political process, and individual hearings for everyone would be inefficient.

Outline 5.5

column1: For a due-process question, which definition of "rule" do you use?
column2:
The common-law Bi-Metallic/Londoner one.

Outline 5.7

column1: For choosing an APA quadrant, which definition of "rule" do you use?
column2:
§ 551(4).

Outline 5.7

column1: What does § 559 say about other procedural law?
column2:
The APA does not repeal or limit extra procedures required by other statutes or law.

Outline 5.7

column1: Which White House office reviews significant rules for cost-benefit before they take effect?
column2:
OIRA (in OMB).

Outline 5.6

column1: Name four of the six sources of agency procedural obligations.
column2:
Any four of: the APA, the organic statute, the Constitution, the agency's own regulations, past practice, judicial gloss.

Outline 5.1

column1: What statutory words trigger formal APA procedures?
column2:
"On the record after opportunity for an agency hearing."

Outline 6.2

column1: Which case held "after hearing" alone does not trigger formal rulemaking?
column2:
United States v. Florida East Coast Ry. (1973)

Case Bank E

column1: In Florida East Coast, what procedure did the ICC use instead of oral hearings?
column2:
Written submissions.

Case Bank E

column1: Under § 556(d), who bears the burden of proof?
column2:
The proponent of the rule or order.

Appendix B, § 556

column1: Under § 554(d), what can't the presiding officer do?
column2:
Consult anyone ex parte on a fact in issue, or be supervised by investigators or prosecutors.

Outline 7.1

column1: Under § 557(b), when does an ALJ's initial decision become the agency's decision?
column2:
Automatically, unless it is appealed or reviewed.

Outline 7.2

column1: Under § 557(b), what power does the agency have when reviewing an initial decision?
column2:
All the powers it would have had in deciding initially.

Outline 7.2

column1: Is a statutory "hearing" formal? Option 1 of 3:
column2:
Presume informal (City of West Chicago v. NRC, 7th Cir.).

Outline 7.3

column1: Is a statutory "hearing" formal? Option 2 of 3:
column2:
Presume formal (Seacoast Anti-Pollution League v. Costle, 1st Cir.).

Outline 7.3

column1: Is a statutory "hearing" formal? Option 3 of 3:
column2:
Defer to the agency's reasonable reading (Chemical Waste Management v. EPA, D.C. Cir.).

Outline 7.3

column1: Which of the three formal-hearing options is the majority view?
column2:
Defer to the agency (Chemical Waste).

Outline 7.3

column1: Why does Chemical Waste survive Loper Bright?
column2:
Statutory stare decisis protects cases decided under Chevron.

Case Bank E

column1: In Seacoast, what did the EPA Administrator improperly rely on?
column2:
A study outside the hearing record.

Case Bank E

column1: City of West Chicago involved what kind of NRC action?
column2:
A license amendment to store thorium-contaminated soil.

column1: § 553 notice-and-comment, step 1 of 3:

Notice in the Federal Register.

column1: § 553 notice-and-comment, step 2 of 3:
column2:
Opportunity for written comment (oral optional).

Outline 8.1

column1: § 553 notice-and-comment, step 3 of 3:
column2:
A concise general statement of basis and purpose.

Outline 8.1

column1: What two trial-type procedures does § 553 not require?
column2:
A hearing and cross-examination.

Outline 8.1

column1: Under § 553(d), how long before its effective date must a substantive rule generally be published?

30 days.

column1: Which case barred courts from adding rulemaking procedures beyond the APA?
column2:
Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. NRDC (1978)

column1: What extra procedure had the D.C. Circuit effectively demanded in Vermont Yankee?
column2:
Cross-examination.

Adequate notice: disclose the data that animated the agency.

Logical outgrowth: the final rule can't stray too far from the proposal.

Outline 8.4

Respond to significant comments.

If true, it would require a change in the proposed rule.

They strengthen steps 1 and 3 of § 553, not step 2.

Outline 8.4

column1: What does a substantive (legislative) rule do?
column2:
It creates rights or obligations and has the force of law.

Outline 9.1

column1: What does an interpretive rule do?
column2:
It clarifies rather than creates law. No force of law, no N&C needed.

Outline 9.1

column1: What does a general statement of policy announce?
column2:
The factors or tentative goals the agency will consider, often about enforcement.

Outline 9.1

column1: Guidance vs. legislative rule, test 1 of 3:
column2:
